cards.title: Limiting reactant: divide moles by coefficient
cards.difficulty_signal: 73% correct at HL and 66% at SL; examiners call the SL version highly discriminating. Limiting reactant is the top error phrase in the reports.

evidence.note: Worked question; key D.
Weaker students found the limiting reactant, then skipped the mole ratio for the yield.
Option A was the top distractor: right yield, wrong limiting reactant.
26% assumed Cu limiting and chose the larger yield.
Many struggled to find the limiting reagent and what remained.

1_context.syllabus_hook: R2.1.3: the limiting reactant determines the theoretical yield.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books teach it as a separate step; exams pair the limiting reactant with the yield, so both must agree.

trap_boundaries: An MCQ pair needs both parts right: correct yield with the wrong reactant scores zero.
Equal moles does not mean equal use: coefficients decide.
2_markscheme_logic.delta: Tempting answers get one half of the pair. Full credit needs the ÷coefficient test and then the ratio to the product.

disguises: Equal mole amounts that hide the coefficient effect
Asking what is left after the reaction
Two gases mixed in a stated ratio
3_novel_application.heuristic: Ask how much of B all of A would need, then compare it with what you have.

4_command_terms.score_mechanics: MCQ: one mark, all or nothing. Written answers usually show moles first; later marks can follow by ECF.

5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Do not work out the yield from both reactants once the limiting one is known.

6_data_booklet.hack: The syllabus says Ar values come from the booklet, to two decimals. Coefficients come only from your equation; no booklet table gives them.

rules: If a pair names reactant X, its yield must be what X gives by the ratio.
Yield cannot exceed what the limiting reactant allows.

walkthrough.question:
Magnesium (0.20 mol) is mixed with hydrochloric acid containing 0.20 mol of HCl.
Mg(s) + 2HCl(aq) → MgCl2(aq) + H2(g)
Which pair gives the limiting reactant and the theoretical yield of H2 in mol?
A. Mg, 0.10
B. Mg, 0.20
C. HCl, 0.05
D. HCl, 0.10
walkthrough.key_idea: Smallest moles ÷ coefficient limits; its ratio then sets the product.
walkthrough.careful: Equal moles still leave one reactant limiting; check the coefficients.
procedure: Write the balanced equation.
Find the moles of each reactant.
Divide each reactant's moles by its coefficient.
The smallest result is the limiting reactant.
Use the limiting reactant's ratio to find product moles.
tricks: Equal moles: the reactant with the larger coefficient limits.
Check a pair: the yield must fit the named reactant's ratio.
if_lost: How many HCl does one Mg need?
How much HCl would all the Mg need?
Is that much HCl available?
What ratio links HCl to H2?

1_context.short: Limiting reactant sets the yield; this asks for both.
1_context.why: Product stops when one reactant runs out, so only that reactant's moles can set the yield.
1_context.avoid: Stopping once the limiting reactant is named; weaker students did this (25M.1A.HL.6213.23).
1_context.syllabus_hook: R2.1.3: the limiting reactant determines the theoretical yield.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books practise the two steps apart; this tests them as one linked pair.

2_markscheme_logic.short: HCl limits, and 2 HCl gives 1 H2.
2_markscheme_logic.why: The key needs both halves. HCl has a coefficient of 2, so 0.20 mol is used twice as fast as Mg.
2_markscheme_logic.avoid: Option A: right yield, wrong limiting reactant, the top distractor (25M.1A.SL.TZ2.18).
2_markscheme_logic.trap_boundary: The mark needs the correct reactant and correct yield together.
2_markscheme_logic.delta: A has the yield but names Mg. C names HCl but halves the ratio twice. Only D has both.

3_novel_application.short: Equal moles look balanced, but the coefficients are not.
3_novel_application.why: Moles are only comparable after dividing by coefficients, as the equation sets the rate of use.
3_novel_application.avoid: Assuming neither limits because both amounts are 0.20 mol.
3_novel_application.disguise: Both reactants have the same number of moles, which hides the limiting reactant.
3_novel_application.heuristic: Ask: if all of the Mg reacted, would there be enough HCl?

4_command_terms.short: No command term: one mark for the full pair.
4_command_terms.why: Each distractor is built from one correct step, so half-finished thinking still finds an option.
4_command_terms.avoid: Choosing the first option that has your first result.
4_command_terms.demands: Pick the one option with the correct limiting reactant and correct yield.
4_command_terms.score_mechanics: All or nothing: one mark for the correct pair.

5_time_efficiency.short: Two divisions and one ratio, about 30 seconds.
5_time_efficiency.why: The second division settles the limiting reactant, and its value is already the H2 amount here.
5_time_efficiency.avoid: Calculating a yield from both reactants.
5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: No masses or molar masses are needed; everything is already in moles.

6_data_booklet.short: No booklet needed: the amounts are already in moles.
6_data_booklet.why: Ar values only matter when masses must become moles. This ratio comes from the equation.
6_data_booklet.avoid: Looking up Mg and Cl values you will not use.
6_data_booklet.pattern: None here: the equation's coefficients do all the work.
6_data_booklet.memorise: Coefficients are read from the balanced equation; no booklet table supplies them.

7_elimination.short: Options A and B need more HCl than exists.
7_elimination.why: If Mg limited, all 0.20 mol would need 0.40 mol HCl, and only 0.20 mol is present.

definitely_wrong.rule: Mg cannot limit: it would need twice the HCl present.
Mg cannot limit, for the same reason.
0.20 mol HCl gives half as much H2, not a quarter.

walkthrough.answer: D. HCl is limiting (0.20 ÷ 2 = 0.10, below Mg's 0.20 ÷ 1), giving 0.10 mol H2.

cards.title: Limiting reactant with mixed units
cards.difficulty_signal: Less than 60% at HL and about half at SL; examiners noted concern about the mental arithmetic needed.

evidence.note: Worked question; key C.
Under 60% found the limiting reagent and maximum yield.
Half used the limiting reactant correctly.
Using 22.7 at non-STP conditions lost M2; moles of reactants also went wrong.
Many used a molar volume for the wrong conditions.
Most common error: kilograms not converted to grams before finding moles.
Some did not convert cm3 to dm3.
Wrong initial amount and missing mole ratio were common; an answer also lost its mark for not using the units requested.

1_context.syllabus_hook: R2.1.2 and R2.1.3: mole ratios with masses and volumes; the limiting reactant sets the yield.
1_context.textbook_gap: Book examples often use one unit; exams give each reactant in a different unit, so converting comes first.

trap_boundaries: 22.7 dm3 mol-1 applies only at STP: outside STP it cost a mark (24M.2.SL.TZ1.1).
Give the answer in the units requested, even when the working is right (16M.2.SL.TZ0.1).
2_markscheme_logic.delta: Partial credit often comes by ECF after a slip. Full credit needs correct conversions, the correct limiting reactant and the ratio.

disguises: A mass with a gas volume
Kilograms or cm3 instead of g or dm3
Asking which gases remain after a gas reaction
3_novel_application.heuristic: Before comparing anything, turn every quantity into moles.

4_command_terms.score_mechanics: MCQ: all or nothing. Written answers: marks for moles, the limiting reactant and the final value, with ECF.

5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Round friendly numbers in an MCQ; here 0.05 and 0.2 are enough to separate the options.

6_data_booklet.hack: The syllabus says Ar values come from the booklet, to two decimals. This question prints the molar volume. Use it only at the stated conditions.

rules: Product mass cannot exceed the combined mass of reactants.
Option values often match a skipped ratio or wrong limiting reactant: check them last.

walkthrough.question:
A sample of 4.60 g of sodium reacts with 1.14 dm3 of chlorine gas at STP, where the molar volume is 22.7 dm3 mol-1.
2Na(s) + Cl2(g) → 2NaCl(s)
What mass of sodium chloride, in g, can form?
A. 1.17
B. 2.92
C. 5.84
D. 11.7
walkthrough.key_idea: Convert mass and volume to moles, then compare by coefficients.
walkthrough.careful: Use the Cl2 to NaCl ratio after finding the limiting reactant.
procedure: Turn mass into moles using molar mass.
Turn gas volume into moles using molar volume.
Divide each by its coefficient.
Smallest result is the limiting reactant.
Use its ratio to find product moles.
Multiply product moles by molar mass.
tricks: Round for mental work: compare 4.6/23 with 1.14/22.7.
Check: product mass cannot exceed total reactant mass.
if_lost: Which units do the two reactants use?
How do you turn each into moles?
Which reactant runs out first?
How many NaCl form per Cl2?

1_context.short: Two units, one limiting reactant, and the answer in grams.
1_context.why: Masses and volumes cannot be compared directly. Only moles count particles, and the equation works in particles.
1_context.syllabus_hook: R2.1.3: identify limiting and excess reactants; R2.1.2: reacting masses and volumes.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books often show one unit per example; this mixes grams and dm3 in one line.

2_markscheme_logic.short: Cl2 limits: about 0.05 mol gives about 0.10 mol NaCl.
2_markscheme_logic.why: Na gives 0.20 ÷ 2 = 0.10, and Cl2 gives about 0.05 ÷ 1. The smaller value decides the product.
2_markscheme_logic.avoid: Skipping the limiting check; under 60% found the yield (24N.1.HL.TZ0.3).
2_markscheme_logic.trap_boundary: Using Na as limiting gives option D, which assumes more chlorine than exists.
2_markscheme_logic.delta: D uses all the sodium. C uses all the chlorine, the true limit, with two NaCl per Cl2.

3_novel_application.short: The gas volume is just moles in disguise.
3_novel_application.why: At STP each mole occupies 22.7 dm3, so dividing by it gives moles, like dividing mass by molar mass.
3_novel_application.avoid: Using 22.7 at other conditions, which lost marks (24M.2.SL.TZ1.1).
3_novel_application.disguise: A solid mass and a gas volume look like different kinds of problem.
3_novel_application.heuristic: Ask: what would each number be in moles?

4_command_terms.short: No command term: one mark, four numeric options.
4_command_terms.why: Options come from common slips, so a slip usually lands on a printed value. Matching is not proof.
4_command_terms.avoid: Trusting an answer only because it appears in the list.
4_command_terms.demands: Select the maximum mass of product from the given amounts.
4_command_terms.score_mechanics: All or nothing: one mark for the correct mass.

5_time_efficiency.short: Round the moles and finish in about 60 seconds.
5_time_efficiency.why: The options differ by factors of about two, so rounded moles are enough to separate them.
5_time_efficiency.avoid: Long division that uses up time; examiners noted the arithmetic load (24N.1.HL.TZ0.3).
5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Skip the excess sodium remaining; the question does not ask for it.

6_data_booklet.short: Molar volume is printed; take Na and Cl values from Ar.
6_data_booklet.why: The syllabus says to use booklet Ar values to two decimals, which gives the molar mass 58.44 for NaCl.
6_data_booklet.avoid: Using rounded Ar values in a written calculation.
6_data_booklet.pattern: Na 22.99 plus Cl 35.45 gives NaCl 58.44, using the booklet's Ar values as the syllabus directs.
6_data_booklet.memorise: Moles from gas volume is volume ÷ molar volume. Booklet section text was not supplied, so no number is cited.

7_elimination.short: 11.7 g is more than all the reactants combined.
7_elimination.why: Mass is conserved. About 3.5 g of chlorine plus 4.60 g of sodium gives about 8 g at most.
7_elimination.avoid: Picking D because it uses the full sodium mass.

definitely_wrong.rule: It exceeds the combined mass of the reactants.
It treats each Cl2 as giving one NaCl, not two.

walkthrough.answer: C. Na is 0.20 mol and Cl2 about 0.05 mol, so Cl2 limits. About 0.10 mol NaCl × 58.44 is about 5.84 g; exact Cl2 moles give 5.87 g, closest to C.

cards.title: Follow the mole ratio through two-step reactions
cards.difficulty_signal: 2025 HL paper question with no statistics published; multi-step ratio work appears in a 2025 Paper 2 yield markscheme too.

evidence.note: Worked question; key C.
Theoretical yield uses a coefficient of 2 in the mass ratio.
Some divided or multiplied by 2 wrongly even with a correct equation.
A significant number chose an option that ignored the mole ratio.

1_context.syllabus_hook: R2.1.2: use the mole ratio to determine masses of reactants and products.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books usually use one equation; exams can link two, so a product of one is the reactant of the next.

trap_boundaries: Excess reactant data is not used for the yield.
Multiplying or dividing by 2 the wrong way is a common slip even with a correct equation.
2_markscheme_logic.delta: Tempting answers miss or invert the factor of 2. Full credit multiplies ratios across both steps.

disguises: Intermediate salt linking two equations
Excess reactant named in words
Ratio hidden in a compound's formula
3_novel_application.heuristic: Follow one substance from start to finish, writing the ratio at each arrow.

4_command_terms.score_mechanics: MCQ: all or nothing. Written: one mark for theoretical mass, one for what follows; a correct final answer earns both.

5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Ignore by-products such as water and carbon dioxide; they do not affect the chain.

6_data_booklet.hack: The question prints both Mr values here. When it does not, the syllabus says to build them from the booklet's Ar values.

rules: Moles doubling means the product mass cannot equal the 1:1 result.
Mass ratio inverted gives a value that often appears as an option.

walkthrough.question:
Ethanamide is made from 4.00 g of ammonium carbonate and excess ethanoic acid in two steps.
2CH3COOH(l) + (NH4)2CO3(s) → 2CH3COONH4(aq) + H2O(l) + CO2(g)
CH3COONH4(aq) → CH3CONH2(s) + H2O(l)
Mr of (NH4)2CO3 is 96.11 and Mr of CH3CONH2 is 59.08.
What is the theoretical yield of ethanamide, in g?
A. 1.23
B. 2.46
C. 4.92
D. 6.51
walkthrough.key_idea: One ammonium carbonate gives two ethanamide through the chain.
walkthrough.question_type: Mole ratio: find amount of another substance
walkthrough.careful: Multiply ratios along the chain; do not stop after one step.
procedure: Find moles of the substance with known quantity.
Write the ratio for each linked equation.
Multiply ratios to link start and final product.
Find moles of the final product.
Multiply by the final product's molar mass.
tricks: Cancel the intermediate: 1 carbonate gives 2 salt gives 2 amide.
Quick estimate: mass × (Mr product ÷ Mr reactant) × ratio.
if_lost: Which reactant has a known amount?
What does each mole of it form in step one?
What does that substance form in step two?
What links your moles to mass?

1_context.short: Link two equations through the salt they share.
1_context.why: The salt made in step one is what step two uses, so its moles carry across.
1_context.avoid: Applying a 1:1 ratio because the second equation is 1:1.
1_context.syllabus_hook: R2.1.2: mole ratios determine masses of reactants and products.
1_context.textbook_gap: Book yield problems usually use one equation; this needs a chain of two.

2_markscheme_logic.why: Step one doubles moles and step two keeps them, so the overall ratio is 1:2.
2_markscheme_logic.avoid: Multiplying or dividing by 2 the wrong way (12M.2.HL.TZ2.2).
2_markscheme_logic.trap_boundary: Ethanoic acid is in excess, so its coefficient does not enter the calculation.
2_markscheme_logic.delta: B stops at 1:1, A divides by 2, and D inverts the Mr ratio. C applies 1:2 correctly.

3_novel_application.short: Two-step synthesis looks harder, but it is one ratio.
3_novel_application.why: Multiplying ratios cancels the intermediate, leaving start and end. The maths is one equation's work.
3_novel_application.avoid: Trying to track water or carbon dioxide.
3_novel_application.disguise: The unfamiliar organic route hides a simple overall ratio.
3_novel_application.heuristic: Ask: per one start unit, how many final units form?

4_command_terms.short: No command term: one mark, numeric options.
4_command_terms.why: Each option comes from one slip in the ratio or Mr, so only the full chain reaches the key.
4_command_terms.avoid: Accepting 2.46 because it follows from the printed Mr values.
4_command_terms.demands: Select the maximum mass of ethanamide available from the known reactant.
4_command_terms.score_mechanics: All or nothing: one mark for the correct mass.

5_time_efficiency.short: Three moves, about 40 seconds with a calculator.
5_time_efficiency.why: Ratios combine first, so only one division and one multiplication remain.
5_time_efficiency.avoid: Writing out an amount for the salt and each product.
5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Skip by-products and the excess acid; they do not affect this yield.

6_data_booklet.short: Both Mr values are printed in the question.
6_data_booklet.why: Printed values are the ones the options were built from, so no booklet lookup is needed.
6_data_booklet.avoid: Recalculating Mr from Ar values and adding rounding differences.
6_data_booklet.pattern: None here: use the Mr values given in the stem.
6_data_booklet.memorise: How to read ratios across linked equations: no booklet table covers this.

7_elimination.short: Doubled moles rule out anything at or below 1:1.
7_elimination.why: At 1:1 the mass is about 0.6 × 4 g. Doubling moles must exceed that.
7_elimination.avoid: Keeping B because it uses all the printed numbers.

definitely_wrong.rule: It halves moles though the chain doubles them.
It ignores the 2 in the first equation.
It multiplies by the Mr ratio upside down.

cards.title: Mole ratio between two substances
cards.difficulty_signal: 90% correct: a safe mark, but mole-ratio slips still recur in harder calculations.

evidence.note: Worked question; key C.
90% deduced one product's amount from another's.
A significant number ignored the mole ratio.
The majority used the ratio correctly to find a reactant amount.

1_context.syllabus_hook: R2.1.2: the mole ratio of an equation determines amounts of reactants and products.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books usually link a reactant to a product; exams may link two products.

trap_boundaries: Use both coefficients as a fraction, never one alone.
The ratio must run from the known to the unknown.
2_markscheme_logic.delta: Wrong options use one coefficient or invert the fraction. The key uses wanted ÷ known.

disguises: Two products rather than reactant and product
An unfamiliar compound such as a nitride
3_novel_application.heuristic: Ignore the chemistry: read only the two coefficients you need.

4_command_terms.score_mechanics: MCQ: all or nothing for one mark.

5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Do not find molar masses; the amount is already in moles.

6_data_booklet.hack: No booklet data needed. Coefficients come from the printed equation, and amounts are already in moles.

rules: If the wanted coefficient is larger than the known one, the answer must exceed the given amount.

walkthrough.question:
Magnesium nitride reacts with water.
Mg3N2(s) + 6H2O(l) → 3Mg(OH)2(aq) + 2NH3(aq)
The reaction gives 0.50 mol of ammonia. How much magnesium hydroxide, in mol, forms with it?
A. 0.25
B. 0.33
C. 0.75
D. 1.5
walkthrough.key_idea: Multiply known moles by wanted coefficient over known coefficient.
walkthrough.question_type: Mole ratio: find amount of another substance
walkthrough.careful: Put the wanted substance's coefficient on top of the fraction.
procedure: Find the coefficients of both substances.
Write the fraction: wanted over known.
Multiply the known moles by the fraction.
tricks: Bigger coefficient for the wanted substance means the answer is bigger.
if_lost: Which two substances does the question link?
What are their coefficients?
Should the wanted amount be larger or smaller than the known one?

1_context.short: Two products linked only by their coefficients.
1_context.why: Coefficients count particles for every substance in an equation, so any two can be compared.
1_context.avoid: Looking for a reactant to start from.
1_context.syllabus_hook: R2.1.2: the mole ratio of an equation determines amounts.
1_context.textbook_gap: Book examples usually go reactant to product; this goes product to product.

2_markscheme_logic.short: Three Mg(OH)2 per two NH3, so multiply by 3/2.
2_markscheme_logic.why: For each 2 mol of NH3 there are 3 mol of Mg(OH)2, so 0.50 mol scales to 0.75 mol.
2_markscheme_logic.avoid: Ignoring the mole ratio, as many did (14N.1.HL.TZ0.2).
2_markscheme_logic.trap_boundary: Using one coefficient alone or inverting the fraction misses the mark.
2_markscheme_logic.delta: B inverts the fraction to 2/3; the key uses 3/2.

3_novel_application.short: Unfamiliar nitride, but only two coefficients matter.
3_novel_application.why: The ratio does not depend on the compounds' properties, so unfamiliar names cannot change the method.
3_novel_application.avoid: Being put off by a compound you have not met.
3_novel_application.disguise: An unfamiliar reaction of magnesium nitride.
3_novel_application.heuristic: Cover the rest of the equation; keep only the two terms asked about.

4_command_terms.short: No command term: one mark for one number.
4_command_terms.why: The inverted and single-coefficient slips are all printed, so reasoning decides it, not recognition.
4_command_terms.demands: Select the amount from the mole ratio.
4_command_terms.score_mechanics: All or nothing: one mark.

5_time_efficiency.why: The stem gives moles and a balanced equation, so no conversions are needed.
5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Water and the nitride are irrelevant to this question.

6_data_booklet.why: Everything is in moles and the equation is given, so no molar masses are involved.
6_data_booklet.avoid: Looking up Mg, O and H.
6_data_booklet.pattern: None: read the coefficients from the printed equation.
6_data_booklet.memorise: Set up the ratio as wanted coefficient over known coefficient.

7_elimination.short: Answer must exceed 0.50, because 3 is more than 2.
7_elimination.why: More Mg(OH)2 than NH3 forms, so anything below the given 0.50 cannot be right.

definitely_wrong.rule: It is below 0.50, though more Mg(OH)2 forms than NH3.
It is below 0.50: the fraction has been inverted.
It multiplies by 3 and ignores the coefficient of NH3.

cards.title: Balancing combustion: count the oxygen in the fuel
cards.difficulty_signal: 77% correct, but balanced equations are flagged as difficult across many sessions and cost marks in many options questions.

evidence.note: Worked question; key C.
Most common mistake: not counting ethanol's oxygen, leading to D.
Incorrect oxygen coefficients and wrong combustion products.
MgCl written for magnesium chloride.
30% failed a balanced equation; MgOH and MgCl were written.
Equation written with state symbols: HCl(aq), H2O(l).
Under half used state symbols correctly; HCl(l) and H2O(g) appeared.
Propene combustion coefficients; key D.
Sum of coefficients for iron(II) sulfide; key D.

1_context.syllabus_hook: R2.1.1: deduce chemical equations, including state symbols.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books practise hydrocarbons; exams add oxygen in the fuel, a lowest-whole-number rule or a sum of coefficients.

trap_boundaries: Check formulas first: MgCl and MgOH are wrong (17N.3.HL.TZ0.2).
State symbols must be correct when asked: HCl is aq, not l (18M.3.SL.TZ1.2).
2_markscheme_logic.delta: One mark can be lost when an equation has the right products but is unbalanced. Full credit needs correct formulas, balance and any states.

disguises: Oxygen inside the fuel
Sum of coefficients rather than one coefficient
An odd number of oxygen atoms that forces doubling
3_novel_application.heuristic: Balance oxygen last, and subtract any oxygen already in the fuel.

4_command_terms.score_mechanics: MCQ: one mark. Written equation: often all or nothing, or separate marks for formulas and balancing.

5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: No masses or moles needed; only atom counts matter.

6_data_booklet.hack: Not in a booklet table: you must know that complete combustion gives CO2 and H2O, and ion charges for formulas.

rules: A coefficient that leaves oxygen unequal on each side is out.
Combustion of a hydrocarbon with oxygen-free products is impossible; expect CO2 and H2O.

walkthrough.question:
Ethanol, C2H5OH, burns completely in oxygen to give carbon dioxide and water.
When balanced with the smallest whole numbers, what is the coefficient of O2?
A. 1
B. 2
C. 3
D. 7
walkthrough.key_idea: Oxygen needed from O2 equals product oxygen minus the fuel's oxygen.
walkthrough.question_type: Balance an equation: find a coefficient
walkthrough.careful: Count the oxygen atom inside the fuel when balancing.
procedure: Write correct formulas for all substances.
Balance carbon, then hydrogen.
Count the total oxygen atoms in products.
Subtract oxygen already in the fuel.
Halve the remainder to get O2.
tricks: For CxHyOH: O2 coefficient is (2x + (y+1)/2 − 1) ÷ 2.
Fractions: double every coefficient. Fails only if none needed.
if_lost: How many CO2 does each ethanol give?
How many H2O?
How many O atoms are on the right?
How many of those does ethanol supply?

1_context.short: Combustion equation with an oxygen hidden in the fuel.
1_context.why: Atoms are conserved, so every oxygen source on the left counts, including the fuel's.
1_context.syllabus_hook: R2.1.1: deduce equations when reactants and products are specified.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books mainly balance hydrocarbons; ethanol adds one oxygen to the left side.

2_markscheme_logic.why: Products hold 4 + 3 = 7 O atoms. Ethanol gives 1, so O2 supplies 6, which is 3 O2.
2_markscheme_logic.avoid: Ignoring ethanol's oxygen, the commonest error, leading to D (25M.1A.SL.TZ2.17).
2_markscheme_logic.trap_boundary: The coefficient is for the O2 molecule, not for oxygen atoms.
2_markscheme_logic.delta: D counts seven product oxygens and stops. C subtracts the fuel's oxygen and halves.

3_novel_application.short: A familiar combustion, with a fuel that brings its own oxygen.
3_novel_application.why: Any oxygen-containing fuel works the same way, so the subtraction applies to all alcohols.
3_novel_application.disguise: It looks like ordinary hydrocarbon balancing.
3_novel_application.heuristic: Ask: does the fuel's formula contain oxygen?

4_command_terms.short: No command term: one mark for one coefficient.
4_command_terms.why: Coefficient questions test the whole balance without a written equation, so one slip means no mark.
4_command_terms.avoid: Answering with the number of oxygen atoms.
4_command_terms.demands: Balance the equation and report the O2 coefficient only.
4_command_terms.score_mechanics: All or nothing: one mark.

5_time_efficiency.why: Carbon and hydrogen fix the products immediately, so oxygen is the last and only sum.
5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: No state symbols or masses are needed for this mark.

6_data_booklet.short: No booklet help: know the combustion products.
6_data_booklet.why: Complete combustion products are chemical knowledge. Atom counting needs no data.
6_data_booklet.pattern: None: count atoms from the formulas.
6_data_booklet.memorise: Complete combustion of carbon compounds gives CO2 and H2O.

7_elimination.short: A and B leave far too little oxygen on the left.
7_elimination.why: Products need 7 O atoms. A provides 3 and B provides 5, so oxygen does not balance.
7_elimination.avoid: Picking 7 because it is the product oxygen count.

definitely_wrong.rule: Provides 3 O atoms; products need more.
Provides 5 O atoms; products need more.
It treats the 7 product oxygens as the O2 coefficient.

walkthrough.answer: C. C2H5OH + 3O2 → 2CO2 + 3H2O; the coefficient of O2 is 3.

cards.title: Atom economy: calculate with the formula
cards.difficulty_signal: Reports say most candidates score it in 2025, though it was flagged as difficult in November 2016.

evidence.note: Worked question; key C.
Well understood; most scored the mark.

1_context.syllabus_hook: R2.1.5: calculate atom economy from the stoichiometry of a reaction.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books stress the definition; exams can test it with by-product sizes that let you estimate quickly.

trap_boundaries: Bottom line uses all reactants, not just one.
Atom economy does not use masses measured in an experiment.
2_markscheme_logic.delta: Tempting answers use the wrong denominator or the wrong pair. Full credit uses desired product over all reactants.

disguises: Named organic reaction rather than an atom economy heading
All four molar masses printed, including the by-product
Coefficients greater than 1 in other questions
3_novel_application.heuristic: Find the desired product, then total everything on the left.

4_command_terms.score_mechanics: MCQ: all or nothing for one mark.

5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Do not use the by-product's molar mass in the formula.

6_data_booklet.hack: The syllabus says the atom economy equation is in the booklet, and this question prints it. Booklet section text was not supplied, so no number is cited.

rules: If the desired product's mass is more than the by-products' total, atom economy is above 50%.
Any real by-product rules out values near 100%.

walkthrough.question:
Chloroethane forms when ethane reacts with chlorine.
C2H6(g) + Cl2(g) → C2H5Cl(g) + HCl(g)
Molar masses in g mol-1: C2H6 30.08, Cl2 70.90, C2H5Cl 64.52, HCl 36.46.
Atom economy % = (molar mass of desired product ÷ molar mass of all reactants) × 100.
What is the atom economy?
A. 15.7%
B. 46.6%
C. 63.9%
D. 99.9%
walkthrough.key_idea: Desired product's molar mass over the total molar mass of reactants.
walkthrough.careful: Put all reactants underneath, multiplied by their coefficients.
procedure: Identify the desired product.
Add molar masses of all reactants, using coefficients.
Divide the desired product's molar mass by this total.
Multiply by 100.
tricks: Desired product heavier than by-products means above 50%.
Reactant total equals product total, a quick check on the denominator.
if_lost: Which product does the question want?
Which masses go on the bottom line?
Is the desired product more or less than half the total?

1_context.short: Atom economy measures how much reactant mass ends up as product.
1_context.why: Atoms not in the desired product are waste, so atom economy falls as wastage rises.
1_context.syllabus_hook: R2.1.5: atom economy measures efficiency in green chemistry.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books present a formula; exams print it and reward a quick, correct substitution.

2_markscheme_logic.why: The formula compares the wanted product with everything put in, and that total is 100.98.
2_markscheme_logic.trap_boundary: Use the reactants' total on the bottom; ethane and chloroethane alone give a wrong printed value.
2_markscheme_logic.delta: B compares ethane with chloroethane. C divides chloroethane by the total of both reactants.

3_novel_application.short: Four molar masses printed, but only three are needed.
3_novel_application.why: Conservation of mass makes reactant and product totals equal, so the by-product's value is not needed.
3_novel_application.heuristic: Ask: which values belong in the formula?

4_command_terms.short: No command term: one mark, and formula provided.
4_command_terms.why: The formula is printed, so the only test is which masses go where.
4_command_terms.demands: Substitute correct values into the given formula and select the result.
4_command_terms.score_mechanics: All or nothing: one mark.

5_time_efficiency.why: The bottom total is close to 100, so the answer is about 64%, and only one option fits.
5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Skip the HCl value and exact division.

6_data_booklet.short: Equation is printed here; syllabus says it is in the booklet.
6_data_booklet.why: Atom economy is the one formula the syllabus explicitly says is given, so memorising it adds little.
6_data_booklet.pattern: Read the printed formula in the stem.
6_data_booklet.memorise: Use coefficients in the denominator; section number not available in the supplied text.

7_elimination.short: Product heavier than HCl means above 50%, but not near 100%.
7_elimination.why: Reactant mass splits into 64.52 and 36.46. The larger share is desired, so it is over half, but HCl is real waste.
7_elimination.avoid: Choosing 99.9% because it looks like an efficient process.

definitely_wrong.rule: Below 50%, though the desired product outweighs the by-product.
Below 50%, though the desired product outweighs the by-product.
HCl is a substantial by-product, so it cannot be near 100%.

cards.title: Atom economy of 100%: one product only
cards.difficulty_signal: Just over two-thirds correct in 2025; a concept check needing no calculation.

evidence.note: Worked question; key A.
Just over 2/3 realised that a single product means 100.
Few candidates mentioned atom economy correctly in a green chemistry answer.

1_context.syllabus_hook: R2.1.5: atom economy and its inverse relationship with wastage.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books stress the calculation; exams test the idea with no numbers.

trap_boundaries: A useful by-product still counts against atom economy in the formula.
High yield is not the same as high atom economy.
2_markscheme_logic.delta: Tempting answers use familiar industrial reactions. The key has no second product.

disguises: Same desired product via different routes
Reversible arrow as a distractor
Fermentation or hydrolysis described as green
3_novel_application.heuristic: Count the products in each option; ignore everything else.

4_command_terms.score_mechanics: MCQ: all or nothing. In written green chemistry parts, name atom economy precisely and link it to waste.

5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Do not calculate any molar masses.

6_data_booklet.hack: No booklet lookup needed. The syllabus says the booklet gives the equation; with one product, top and bottom are equal.

rules: Any option with a second product is below 100%.
Exception check: the coefficient of a single product does not matter.

walkthrough.question:
Four routes make ethanol. Which has an atom economy of 100%?
A. C2H4 + H2O → C2H5OH
B. C6H12O6 → 2C2H5OH + 2CO2
C. CH3COOC2H5 + NaOH → C2H5OH + CH3COONa
D. CH3COOC2H5 + H2O ⇌ C2H5OH + CH3COOH
walkthrough.key_idea: Only a single-product reaction turns every reactant atom into desired product.
walkthrough.careful: A useful by-product still lowers atom economy.
procedure: Identify the desired product.
Count the products in each equation.
Choose the equation with only the desired product.
tricks: Scan right-hand sides for a plus sign; any plus means below 100%.
if_lost: What does atom economy compare?
Where do all reactant atoms end up at 100%?
How many products does each option form?

1_context.short: Same product, four routes: compare the wasted atoms.
1_context.why: Atom economy falls as more atoms end up outside the desired product, so wastage is the deciding idea.
1_context.avoid: Choosing the route that sounds most natural.
1_context.syllabus_hook: R2.1.5: atom economy is a measure of efficiency in green chemistry.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books compare calculated values; this needs only the equation's form.

2_markscheme_logic.short: A has only one product, so all atoms are kept.
2_markscheme_logic.why: With one product, its mass equals the reactants' total, so the fraction in the formula is exactly 1.
2_markscheme_logic.avoid: Calculating; about a third missed this quick reasoning (25M.1A.HL.6219.25).
2_markscheme_logic.trap_boundary: Any second product means below 100, whatever the yield.
2_markscheme_logic.delta: B, C and D each make a second substance. A makes only ethanol.

3_novel_application.short: Biological and organic reactions hide a simple product count.
3_novel_application.why: The formula looks only at products and reactants, so reaction type or origin cannot change it.
3_novel_application.avoid: Thinking fermentation is greenest because it uses plants.
3_novel_application.disguise: Fermentation and ester hydrolysis look like greener choices.
3_novel_application.heuristic: Cover the reactants; count what is on the right.

4_command_terms.short: No command term: recognise, do not calculate.
4_command_terms.why: Numbers are absent on purpose, so the test is the concept.
4_command_terms.avoid: Working out molar masses for four equations.
4_command_terms.demands: Pick the one equation with no by-product.
4_command_terms.score_mechanics: All or nothing: one mark.

5_time_efficiency.short: Count products: done in ten seconds.
5_time_efficiency.why: The answer depends only on the number of products, which can be read directly.
5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Skip all arithmetic and any thought about conditions or reversibility.

6_data_booklet.short: Booklet equation not needed for this one.
6_data_booklet.why: With one product, top and bottom of the fraction are equal, so no values are needed.
6_data_booklet.memorise: One product means 100%. More by-product means lower atom economy and more waste.

7_elimination.short: B, C and D each make a second product.
7_elimination.why: Atoms that leave as CO2, sodium ethanoate or ethanoic acid are not in ethanol, so atom economy is below 100.
7_elimination.avoid: Keeping D because the arrow is reversible.

definitely_wrong.rule: CO2 is also formed.
Sodium ethanoate is also formed.
Ethanoic acid is also formed.

walkthrough.answer: A. C2H4 + H2O → C2H5OH has one product, so the atom economy is 100%.

cards.title: Changing the excess reactant does not change the yield
cards.difficulty_signal: Examiners describe it as well answered, but a link between rates and stoichiometry; related parts in practical questions discriminate.

evidence.note: Worked question; key B.
Well answered question on rate and stoichiometry.
With marble in excess and HCl limiting, a little extra marble has little effect.
Limiting reagent is the term used when the other reagent is in excess.

1_context.syllabus_hook: R2.1.3: the limiting reactant determines the theoretical yield.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books separate yield and rate; exams put both in one question.

trap_boundaries: More excess reactant can speed a reaction without raising the final amount.
Average rate changes when time changes, even if the total amount does not.
2_markscheme_logic.delta: Tempting answers treat a same-amount reaction as same-rate. Only the total amount stays equal.

disguises: Same mass with different acid concentrations
Extra marble added in a practical question
Comparison of curves for different concentrations
3_novel_application.heuristic: Ask which reactant runs out; that amount alone decides the final amount.

4_command_terms.score_mechanics: MCQ: one mark. In written practical parts, the reason must name the limiting or excess reactant.

5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Do not calculate moles; the excess is stated.

6_data_booklet.hack: No booklet data needed: this is reasoning about limits and rate, with no calculation.

rules: Any option describing speed changes when concentration changes.

walkthrough.question:
Sodium carbonate powder reacts with excess hydrochloric acid.
Na2CO3(s) + 2HCl(aq) → CO2(g) + 2NaCl(aq) + H2O(l)
Reaction I uses 1.0 g of solid with 0.50 mol dm-3 acid. Reaction II uses 1.0 g of solid with 2.0 mol dm-3 acid.
Which quantity is the same in both?
A. Initial rate of reaction
B. Total mass of CO2 produced
C. Total reaction time
D. Average rate of production of CO2
walkthrough.key_idea: The limiting reactant is unchanged, so the total product is unchanged.
walkthrough.question_type: Excess reactant changed: what stays the same
walkthrough.careful: Same final amount does not mean same rate or time.
procedure: Find the limiting and excess reactants.
Check whether the limiting amount changes.
Same limiting amount gives the same total product.
Anything about speed changes with concentration.
tricks: Amount questions follow the limiting reactant; speed questions follow concentration.
if_lost: Which reactant is in excess?
What sets the total amount of product?
Does higher acid concentration affect how fast it reacts?

1_context.short: Compare yield and rate when excess acid changes.
1_context.why: Excess acid never runs out, so its concentration can affect speed but not the final total.
1_context.avoid: Assuming stronger concentration means more product.
1_context.syllabus_hook: R2.1.3: the limiting reactant determines the theoretical yield.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books teach yield and kinetics in different chapters; this tests the difference.

2_markscheme_logic.short: Na2CO3 limits and is equal, so total CO2 is equal.
2_markscheme_logic.why: 1.0 g of solid gives a fixed amount of CO2 once all of it reacts. Acid only changes how quickly.
2_markscheme_logic.trap_boundary: The total stays the same only because acid is stated as excess in both.
2_markscheme_logic.delta: A, C and D describe speed, which differs. B describes the final amount, which does not.

3_novel_application.short: A rates-looking question is really a limiting reactant question.
3_novel_application.why: Three options use rate language, which suggests a kinetics question. The one with amount language is decided by stoichiometry.
3_novel_application.disguise: It looks like a rate question about concentration.
3_novel_application.heuristic: Ask: is this option about how much, or how fast?

4_command_terms.short: No command term: choose the one unchanged quantity.
4_command_terms.why: A single unchanged quantity must be found, and the three speed options share one flaw.
4_command_terms.demands: Identify the quantity independent of acid concentration.
4_command_terms.score_mechanics: All or nothing: one mark.

5_time_efficiency.short: Spot excess, and answer in about 15 seconds.
5_time_efficiency.why: The word 'excess' decides everything, so no calculation is needed.
5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Do not calculate the CO2 mass or acid moles.

6_data_booklet.why: The question only asks whether quantities change, so no value is calculated.
6_data_booklet.avoid: Finding the Mr of sodium carbonate.
6_data_booklet.pattern: None: reason from the stated excess.
6_data_booklet.memorise: The limiting reactant fixes total product; concentration of an excess reactant affects speed.

7_elimination.short: Higher acid concentration changes all three rate options.
7_elimination.why: More concentrated acid reacts faster, so initial rate, time and average rate must all differ.
7_elimination.avoid: Keeping D because the amount of CO2 is the same.

definitely_wrong.rule: Higher concentration raises the initial rate.
A faster reaction finishes in less time.
Same CO2 in less time gives a higher average rate.

walkthrough.answer: B. The 1.0 g of sodium carbonate limits both reactions, so total CO2 is the same.

cards.title: Limiting reactant from a graph
cards.difficulty_signal: Flagged in May 2025 reports: using graphical data to justify which reactant is limiting.

evidence.note: HCl limiting, with a reason from different CO2 mass or final mass; converse accepted.
A related practical part names HCl as limiting and marble in excess.
Written limiting-reagent explanations were a flagged weakness in May 2019 findings.

1_context.syllabus_hook: R2.1.3: identify the limiting and excess reactants from given data.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books give moles to compare; 1B questions give curves, so the evidence is the final mass.

trigger_phrases: final mass would be the same
trap_boundaries: The answer requires both limiting reagent and reason.
Accept the converse: same final mass if NaHCO3 were limiting.
2_markscheme_logic.delta: Naming HCl alone earns nothing. Full credit links different CO2 masses to the changing acid amount.

disguises: Mass-time curves rather than moles
Curves of different concentrations levelling at different heights
A rate experiment that also asks about stoichiometry
3_novel_application.heuristic: Look at where curves level off, not how steep they are.

4_command_terms.score_mechanics: Suggest with a reason: one mark for the reagent and the reason together.

5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Skip initial rates and any mole calculation for this mark.

6_data_booklet.hack: No booklet data needed: the evidence is on the graph.

rules: If the curves end at different final masses, the fixed reactant was not limiting.
If only rate differs and final mass is the same, the fixed reactant limits.

walkthrough.question:
The same mass of solid NaHCO3 reacts with a constant volume of HCl(aq) at three concentrations. A data logger records the mass of the mixture every five seconds.
The graph shows mass, starting about 9 g, against time for 0.5, 1.0 and 1.5 mol dm-3 acid. The curves level off at different final masses: highest for 0.5 mol dm-3, lower for 1.0 mol dm-3.
Suggest, with a reason, which reactant was limiting in the 0.5 and 1.0 mol dm-3 reactions.
walkthrough.key_idea: Final mass depends on the limiting reactant, so differing totals expose it.
walkthrough.careful: Name the limiting reagent and give the reason together.
procedure: Identify which reactant changes between runs.
Compare the final level of each curve.
Link final mass lost to product formed.
Totals change with a reactant: that reactant limits.
tricks: Final levels equal: fixed reactant limits. Final levels differ: changed reactant limits.
Fails when curves have not finished levelling off; read the plateau only.
if_lost: What does the mass loss represent?
Which reactant's amount changed between runs?
What would the final masses do if the solid ran out?

1_context.short: Graph data, not moles, identifies the limiting reactant here.
1_context.why: Mass falls as CO2 escapes, so the mass lost measures product formed and therefore shows what limited it.
1_context.avoid: Assuming concentrated acid can never be limiting.
1_context.syllabus_hook: R2.1.3: identify limiting and excess reactants from given data.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books use mole calculations; here the proof comes from the graph's plateaus.

2_markscheme_logic.short: HCl limits: same solid mass but different CO2 mass.
2_markscheme_logic.why: Fixed solid with changing totals means the solid did not control the total, so the acid did.
trigger_phrases: final mass same if NaHCO3 limiting
2_markscheme_logic.trap_boundary: The single mark needs reagent AND reason; a converse argument is accepted.
2_markscheme_logic.delta: HCl with no reason scores nothing. HCl plus different CO2 or final mass scores the mark.

3_novel_application.short: A rate experiment secretly asks about stoichiometry.
3_novel_application.why: Slope shows speed and plateau shows total amount, so one graph tests both ideas.
3_novel_application.disguise: A mass-time rate graph looks like a kinetics question.
3_novel_application.heuristic: Ask: does this part depend on slope or plateau?

4_command_terms.short: Suggest with a reason: name it, then justify.
4_command_terms.why: Suggest asks for a proposal, and 'with a reason' makes the justification part of the single mark.
4_command_terms.demands: Name the limiting reagent and support it using the graph.
4_command_terms.score_mechanics: One mark, needing the reagent and the reason together.

5_time_efficiency.short: Read the plateaus and write one clear sentence.
5_time_efficiency.why: Only the final levels matter, so the rest of each curve needs no reading.
5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Skip gradients and mole calculations on this part.

6_data_booklet.short: No booklet data needed: the graph holds the evidence.
6_data_booklet.why: This is a comparison of measured totals, so no constants or atomic masses are used.
6_data_booklet.memorise: Mass loss in an open container measures gas escaping, here CO2.

7_elimination.short: NaHCO3 as limiting would give the same final mass.
7_elimination.why: If the solid ran out, each run would make the same CO2 from equal solid, so plateaus would match.

definitely_wrong.rule: Equal solid would give equal mass loss, and the plateaus differ.

definitely_wrong.target: A reason based on speed or slope
definitely_wrong.rule: Slope shows rate, not which reactant ran out.

walkthrough.answer: HCl is limiting. The same mass of solid gave different masses of CO2 and different final masses; if NaHCO3 were limiting, final masses would match.

cards.title: Titration data: endpoint, then concentration
cards.difficulty_signal: Examiners report many could not draw best-fit lines and were imprecise reading the volume; concentration was then mostly correct.

evidence.note: Best-fit lines, 27.0 cm3, range 26.0–28.0, concentration 0.926 mol dm-3; [1 max] without units.
Many could not draw a best-fit line; volume reading imprecise.
Some failed to convert cm3 to dm3.
Candidates struggled to transfer volumetric lab skills.
Titration calculation with ratio and moles then concentration.

1_context.syllabus_hook: R2.1.2: the mole ratio determines concentrations of reactants and products in solution.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books show indicator titrations; exams use temperature lines, and the endpoint must be found from the graph.

trap_boundaries: Volume must match your own annotation, within the accepted range.
Number without units is capped at one mark.
2_markscheme_logic.delta: A correct number alone earns 1 of 2. Full credit needs mol dm-3 units too.

disguises: Temperature graph rather than a burette reading
Redox titration with a stoichiometric ratio not 1:1
A rise and a plateau instead of a colour change
3_novel_application.heuristic: The reaction stops when one reactant runs out: find the change in trend.

4_command_terms.score_mechanics: Marks given per step: lines, volume, working to concentration, and units. A correct final answer with units takes both concentration marks.

5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Do not join points dot to dot; two ruled lines are enough.

6_data_booklet.hack: n = CV is in section 1. Remember volumes must be in dm3, and the mole ratio comes from your equation.

rules: Endpoint volume is beyond the last rising point, not at the highest plotted reading alone.
A 1:1 reaction using more acid volume than base means the acid is less concentrated.

walkthrough.question:
Hydrochloric acid was added in 5.0 cm3 portions to 25.0 cm3 of 1.00 mol dm-3 NaOH, up to 50.0 cm3 of acid, and the temperature was recorded. Both solutions started at the same temperature.
The graph has these approximate points (volume in cm3, temperature in °C): 0, 25.0; 5, 25.8; 10, 27.0; 15, 28.0; 20, 28.8; 25, 29.8; 30, 30.1; 35, 30.0; 40, 30.0; 45, 30.0; 50, 29.8.
(i) Using suitable lines, find the volume of acid that just neutralises the NaOH.
(ii) Find the concentration of the acid, with units.
walkthrough.key_idea: Crossing lines give the endpoint; 1:1 ratio gives the acid concentration.
walkthrough.question_type: Titration data: find endpoint and concentration
walkthrough.careful: Give the final value with mol dm-3 units.
procedure: Draw a best-fit line through each trend.
Read the volume where the lines cross.
Find moles of the known solution using n = CV.
Apply the mole ratio from the balanced equation.
Divide moles by unknown volume in dm3.
State the concentration with units.
tricks: Equal moles in 1:1: C1V1 = C2V2 works in any matching volume units.
Sense check: more acid volume than base means a weaker concentration.
if_lost: Why does temperature stop rising?
What two lines describe the data?
How many moles of NaOH are present?
What is the mole ratio of HCl to NaOH?

1_context.short: Temperature peak marks neutralisation, so read the volume from it.
1_context.why: Heat is released only while both reactants remain, so the trend changes at the endpoint.
1_context.avoid: Reading a volume with no lines; many could not draw them (15M.2.HL.TZ2.1).
1_context.syllabus_hook: R2.1.2: use the mole ratio for concentrations in solution.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books use indicators; this finds the endpoint from a heating curve.

2_markscheme_logic.short: Lines, then 27.0 cm3, then 0.926 mol dm-3 with units.
2_markscheme_logic.why: Equal moles at the endpoint: 0.0250 mol NaOH needs 0.0250 mol HCl in 0.0270 dm3.
2_markscheme_logic.avoid: Omitting units, which caps (ii) at one mark (15M.2.HL.TZ2.1).
2_markscheme_logic.trap_boundary: 26.0–28.0 cm3 is accepted if consistent with your lines; ECF volumes follow the maximum temperature of your line. Give one decimal place.
2_markscheme_logic.delta: Number only earns 1 of 2 in (ii). Number with units earns 2; lines plus volume earn 2 in (i).

3_novel_application.short: A titration with a thermometer, not an indicator.
3_novel_application.why: Any measured property with a sharp trend change can show the endpoint, so the method transfers.
3_novel_application.avoid: Assuming endpoints always need a colour change.
3_novel_application.disguise: A temperature graph hides the titration.
3_novel_application.heuristic: Ask: at what point does the reaction stop producing change?

4_command_terms.short: Determine: show lines on the graph, then find one value.
4_command_terms.why: Determine wants the only possible answer, with visible evidence, so annotated lines earn marks too.
4_command_terms.avoid: Writing a volume with no annotation.
4_command_terms.demands: Annotate the graph, read the volume, then calculate concentration with units.
4_command_terms.score_mechanics: Per point: lines, volume, working and final concentration; a correct final answer with units earns both (ii) marks.

5_time_efficiency.short: Ruler lines first, then one short calculation.
5_time_efficiency.why: The volume feeds the calculation, so an accurate reading saves corrections later.
5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Skip the balanced equation in full; just state 1:1 for HCl and NaOH.

6_data_booklet.why: The booklet provides the relationship; you still supply the ratio and the unit conversion.
6_data_booklet.avoid: Using cm3 in n = CV without conversion (10M.2.SL.TZ2.1).
6_data_booklet.pattern: Use n = CV for NaOH, then rearrange for the acid.
6_data_booklet.memorise: HCl and NaOH react 1:1, and cm3 ÷ 1000 gives dm3.

7_elimination.short: Rule out volumes before the rise ends and concentrations above 1.
7_elimination.why: Acid volume needed exceeds the 25.0 cm3 of base, so at 1:1 the acid must be less concentrated.
7_elimination.avoid: Reading the highest plotted point as exact.

definitely_wrong.rule: Temperature is still rising at 25 cm3, so neutralisation is not finished.
More acid than base is needed in a 1:1 reaction.
It is limited to one mark in (ii).

walkthrough.answer: (i) Two best-fit lines; about 27.0 cm3 (26.0–28.0 accepted if consistent with the lines). (ii) 1.00 × 0.0250 ÷ 0.0270 = 0.926 mol dm-3.

cards.title: Enthalpy per mole: divide by the limiting reactant
cards.difficulty_signal: In a similar question, most candidates did not divide by moles of limiting reactant; about 40% got the first mass mark.

evidence.note: Q from combined mass, n = 0.0250, ΔH = -45 kJ mol-1; [2] for +45; ECF on M3.
q ÷ moles of limiting CuSO4 gives per-mole value; assumptions listed.
Most did not divide by moles of limiting reactant; incorrect mass in q = mcΔT.

1_context.syllabus_hook: R2.1.3: the limiting reactant sets how much reaction occurs. Links to calorimetry in R1.1.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books give the mole in the calorimetry formula; exams need you to choose it from limiting data.

trap_boundaries: +45 kJ mol-1 earns [2], not [3].
ECF applies for M3 even if M1 mass and ΔT are wrong.
c = 4.2 is accepted.
2_markscheme_logic.delta: Sign decides between 2 and 3 marks. The correct final answer with sign earns all marks.

disguises: Thermometric titration with one volume found from a graph
Metal displacement where one reactant is excess
Answer requires kJ mol-1 though q is in J
3_novel_application.heuristic: Ask which reactant actually finished; divide by its moles.

4_command_terms.score_mechanics: Three marks: Q, n, and ΔH with sign. A correct final answer earns all three; ECF protects M3.

5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Do not recalculate moles of excess acid.

6_data_booklet.hack: n = CV is in section 1. The markscheme accepts c = 4.18 or 4.2. q = mcΔT is outside the supplied text, so learn it.

rules: Temperature rose, so ΔH must be negative.
A value in thousands of kJ mol-1 signals J and kJ were mixed.

walkthrough.question:
In a thermometric titration, 25.0 cm3 of 1.00 mol dm-3 NaOH was neutralised by 27.0 cm3 of hydrochloric acid, and the temperature rose by 5.2 °C.
Treat the mixture as water with c = 4.18 J g-1 K-1 and density 1.00 g cm-3.
Calculate the enthalpy change of the reaction, in kJ mol-1.
walkthrough.key_idea: Heat from total solution mass, divided by moles of limiting reactant.
walkthrough.question_type: Calorimetry: enthalpy per mole of limiting reactant
walkthrough.careful: Use the combined solution mass, then show negative sign if temperature rises.
procedure: Add solution volumes to get total mass.
Calculate heat using q = mcΔT.
Convert joules to kilojoules.
Find moles of the limiting reactant.
Divide heat by those moles.
Add a negative sign if temperature rises.
tricks: Reasonable check: strong acid-base values sit near -58 here.
Sign check: warmer means negative.
if_lost: What mass of solution is heated?
How many joules does that give?
How many moles actually reacted?
Is the reaction releasing or absorbing heat?

1_context.short: Heat measured from the solution, then scaled per mole reacted.
1_context.why: The experiment reacts a small amount, but ΔH is per mole, so heat must be divided by reacted moles.
1_context.syllabus_hook: R2.1.3: the limiting reactant determines how much reacts; with enthalpy from R1.1.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books supply one reactant amount; here the student must decide which moles to use.

2_markscheme_logic.why: Each step is a mark: heat, moles and ΔH with sign. A correct final answer earns all three.
2_markscheme_logic.avoid: Using 25.0 g as the mass; wrong mass was a main error (18N.2.SL.TZ0.1).
2_markscheme_logic.trap_boundary: +45 kJ mol-1 earns [2]; M3 allows ECF even with wrong mass and ΔT.
2_markscheme_logic.delta: +45 gets 2 of 3. -45 gets all 3.

3_novel_application.short: Neutralisation hides the limiting idea at the equivalence point.
3_novel_application.why: At the endpoint both are used up, so either amount works; NaOH is the known one, so use it.
3_novel_application.avoid: Using the acid's unconfirmed concentration when NaOH is known.
3_novel_application.heuristic: Ask: which amount in moles is known exactly?

4_command_terms.short: Calculate: show steps; the sign and unit are needed.
4_command_terms.why: Calculate expects working; ECF only applies if your method is visible.
4_command_terms.demands: Show q, moles and ΔH in kJ mol-1, with the negative sign.
4_command_terms.score_mechanics: Three marks by steps; a correct final answer earns all, and +45 earns [2].

5_time_efficiency.short: Three short lines of working, under two minutes.
5_time_efficiency.why: Each line carries a mark, so more writing adds nothing, but missing a line risks ECF.
5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Skip percentage error and reasons for heat loss until later parts.

6_data_booklet.short: n = CV is in section 1; c is given here.
6_data_booklet.why: The relationship and heat capacity are the only data needed, and the markscheme accepts both 4.18 and 4.2.
6_data_booklet.avoid: Using the molar mass of NaOH.
6_data_booklet.pattern: Apply n = CV to NaOH with its volume in dm3.
6_data_booklet.memorise: q = mcΔT and the sign rule: warming means negative ΔH.

7_elimination.short: A positive value cannot be right as the mixture warmed.
7_elimination.why: Warming means heat left the reaction, so ΔH is negative, and only the sign separates 2 and 3 marks.

definitely_wrong.rule: Temperature rose, so the reaction is exothermic.
That is q alone, not per mole.

definitely_wrong.target: A value of thousands of kJ mol-1
definitely_wrong.rule: Joules were not converted to kilojoules.

cards.title: Percentage error is not percentage yield
cards.difficulty_signal: May 2024 flagged the confusion between percentage yield and percentage error; significant figures also repeatedly cost marks.

evidence.note: Percentage error 22%, two significant figures required, sign ignored.
Some calculated percentage error instead of percentage yield; significant figures ignored.
Percentage yield calculation was mostly fine; confusion with percentage error followed.
Percentage yield is 100 × actual ÷ theoretical; [2] for correct final answer.
Weaker candidates divided the given masses directly rather than theoretical mass.
Yield by mass or by moles gives near the same percentage.
Candidates failed to realise results above 100% were unrealistic.
More than half did not give the required significant figures.

1_context.syllabus_hook: R2.1.4: percentage yield is the ratio of experimental yield to theoretical yield.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books give both formulas separately; exams place them near each other, and candidates mix them.

trap_boundaries: Percentage error needs the stated significant figures; sign is ignored here.
Percentage yield cannot use a given mass as the theoretical yield until it is calculated.
2_markscheme_logic.delta: Percentage yield uses a ratio; percentage error uses a difference. Each is wrong for the other's question.

disguises: Literature enthalpy value rather than a mass
Yield given as 0.068 from an earlier part
Calculated mass above actual, then above 100%
3_novel_application.heuristic: Ask: am I comparing with the theoretical amount or an accepted value?

4_command_terms.score_mechanics: Often one mark for the final value; significant figures may be required by the question.

5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Do not repeat earlier calculations; use the given value or your answer by ECF.

6_data_booklet.hack: Neither formula appears in the supplied text. Learn both, and check the question's wanted significant figures.

rules: A percentage yield above 100% signals an error to check.
If the literature value is the denominator, it is error, not yield.

walkthrough.question:
A student measures an enthalpy of neutralisation as −45 kJ mol-1. The accepted value is −58 kJ mol-1.
Calculate the percentage error, to two significant figures.
walkthrough.key_idea: Percentage error is difference over literature value, not a yield ratio.
walkthrough.careful: Divide by the literature value, and match the requested significant figures.
procedure: Identify whether the question asks for error or yield.
Subtract the literature value from the experimental value.
Divide by the literature value.
Take the magnitude, then multiply by 100.
Round to the requested significant figures.
tricks: Error: difference ÷ literature. Yield: experimental ÷ theoretical.
Sign is ignored here; check the instruction if a question differs.
if_lost: Which value is the accepted one?
How far is your measurement from it?
What do you divide that gap by?

1_context.short: Compare with an accepted value: this is error, not yield.
1_context.why: Yield compares amount obtained with amount possible; error compares a measurement with an accepted value.
1_context.avoid: Using a yield-style ratio; candidates mixed them up (12N.2.SL.TZ0.1).
1_context.syllabus_hook: R2.1.4: percentage yield is experimental ÷ theoretical; error is its contrast in experiments.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books teach them chapters apart; papers place them side by side.

2_markscheme_logic.why: The gap between -45 and -58 is 13, measured against the accepted 58. Signs cancel in the magnitude.
2_markscheme_logic.avoid: Giving 22.4 %: the answer must be two significant figures.
2_markscheme_logic.trap_boundary: The answer must be 2 s.f.; sign is ignored.
2_markscheme_logic.delta: 22.4 or too many figures loses the mark; 22 earns it.

3_novel_application.short: Enthalpy values, but the percentage method is unchanged.
3_novel_application.why: Percentage error applies to any measured quantity, so kJ mol-1 changes nothing.
3_novel_application.avoid: Thinking the negative signs make it harder.
3_novel_application.heuristic: Ask: where is the accepted value?

4_command_terms.short: Calculate: one mark, one rounded number.
4_command_terms.why: Only one mark is available, so the rounding instruction decides it.
4_command_terms.demands: Obtain the percentage error to two significant figures.
4_command_terms.score_mechanics: One mark for the correct value at the required precision; sign ignored.

5_time_efficiency.short: Three key presses and a rounding check.
5_time_efficiency.why: Earlier parts gave the values, so the work is a single division and a rounding check.
5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Skip explaining the error until the next part asks.

6_data_booklet.short: Formula is not in the supplied text: learn it.
6_data_booklet.why: Both percentage formulas must be recalled here, as no provided booklet text gives them.
6_data_booklet.avoid: Searching for it during the exam.
6_data_booklet.memorise: % error = |experimental − literature| ÷ literature × 100. % yield = experimental ÷ theoretical × 100.

7_elimination.short: Dividing by 45 or quoting three figures loses the mark.
7_elimination.why: The accepted value is the reference, and the question sets the precision.
7_elimination.avoid: Dividing by the experimental value, which gives 29%.

definitely_wrong.rule: That is the ratio 45 ÷ 58, not the error.
It divides by the experimental value.
It has too many significant figures.

cross_links.note: Syllabus guidance places Avogadro's law and molar concentration here; every R2.1 calculation starts by converting to moles.
Calorimetry: heat per mole uses the limiting reactant from R2.1, as in thermometric titrations.
Rate questions often pair with limiting reactant ideas: excess concentration changes speed, not total product.
